## The question behind the tools

**How can a reader trace a business conclusion back to the data and code that produced it?**

Literate programming connects the explanation, instructions, and computed outputs in one readable source.

::: notes
[30 sec] Open with a churn rate on a slide: it is not enough by itself; we also need to explain its denominator, data, and calculation.
:::

## Why reproducibility matters

A result is easier to check when the data, transformations, code, software context, and interpretation are documented together.

- Copied results can become stale after code changes.
- Undocumented cleaning decisions are hard to audit.
- Reproduction requires access to the inputs and a sufficiently specified workflow.

A rendered report alone is not the whole research record [@peng2009; @gandrud2020].

::: notes
[40 sec] Re-running code can reproduce an output given the same inputs and compatible environment; it cannot guarantee valid data or correct reasoning.
:::

## Literate programming: the core idea

Donald Knuth described programming as a form of writing for human readers as well as computers [@knuth1984].

**In a data report:** narrative explains decisions; code makes calculations explicit; output shows what that code produced.

The reader can move from question → method → result → interpretation without switching between disconnected files.

::: notes
[40 sec] The idea predates Quarto. Quarto is one modern publishing system that supports this style; it did not invent literate programming.
:::

## What Quarto does

Quarto is an open-source publishing system. It reads a `.qmd` source and coordinates:

1. Markdown and document metadata
2. Execution of supported code cells (R commonly runs through knitr)
3. Conversion to HTML, PDF, or other publication formats [@quarto]

**Quarto orchestrates the document; R performs R calculations.**

::: notes
[45 sec] Quarto is not a statistical method. The Quarto CLI is the publishing system; the R package `quarto` offers helper functions.
:::

## Quarto and RStudio have different jobs

| Tool | Role in this workflow |
|------|-------------------------------------------|
| R | Reads, transforms, summarises and plots data |
| Quarto | Renders `.qmd` sources into documents |
| RStudio | IDE: edit, run, preview, manage the project |

RStudio can call Quarto’s renderer, but project files can also be rendered from a terminal [@quarto].

::: notes
[40 sec] RStudio is not required for Quarto, and it does not itself calculate R chunks. It provides an integrated interface.
:::

## Anatomy of a `.qmd`

```yaml
---
title: "Churn analysis"
format: html
bibliography: references.bib
csl: apa.csl
---
```

Below the YAML header, Markdown supplies prose and headings. Fenced R chunks contain executable code.

YAML controls **document-level choices**. Chunk options control **what an individual cell shows or executes**.

::: notes
[45 sec] Indentation and colons matter in YAML. Changing output format does not require rewriting the analysis.
:::

## Markdown and executable chunks

Markdown makes structure visible: `##` starts a section, `**text**` is bold, and backticks mark code.

```{r}
#| label: overall-churn
#| echo: true
churn_data <- readr::read_csv("data/customer_churn_simulated.csv",
                              show_col_types = FALSE)
nrow(churn_data)                  # customers in the file
mean(churn_data$churn == "Yes")   # overall churn rate
```

`#|` lines are cell options. `echo` controls code visibility; `eval: false` skips execution; `include: false` runs a cell but hides both code and result. These choices affect display, not analytical validity.

::: notes
[45 sec] This cell really runs when the slides are rendered: 600 customers, 15.7 % churned. `churn == "Yes"` gives TRUE/FALSE, and the mean of TRUE/FALSE values is the share of TRUE. Quarto uses the modern `#|` cell-option syntax. Hiding code does not remove it from the source.
:::

## Rendering: from source to publication

**Edit → execute → convert → inspect**

- In RStudio, use **Render** for the current document.
- From the project folder: `quarto render Tiago_Presentation.qmd`.
- Inspect the generated file; a successful build does not guarantee good layout or valid interpretation.

PDF output needs a working LaTeX engine; this project uses XeLaTeX.

::: notes
[40 sec] A stale PDF is possible if the source is not re-rendered. Inspect the output after every build.
:::

## Citations and APA 7

A BibTeX database stores bibliographic metadata; CSL applies a citation style. Quarto/Pandoc resolves citation keys and builds a reference list.

- YAML: `bibliography: references.bib` and `csl: apa.csl`
- In text: `[@knuth1984]` or `@knuth1984`
- The reference list is generated from cited keys [@quarto]

CSL controls formatting; it cannot verify that a source is real or relevant.

::: notes
[45 sec] Automation reduces formatting work but source titles, dates, DOIs, and interpretations still need human checking.
:::

## Reproducible project structure

```text
project/
  _quarto.yml
  Tiago_Presentation.qmd
  Handout_Quarto.qmd
  references.bib  apa.csl
  data/       # CSV + generator script
  analysis/   # worked churn analysis
  exercise/   # class exercise
```

Use relative paths, record data provenance and cleaning choices, keep a generator for simulated data, and state package requirements. Version control tracks source changes; it does not package every dependency automatically [@gandrud2020].

::: notes
[35 sec] Git preserves file history but does not freeze an R installation or make private data available to another reader.
:::

## Business question: customer churn and revenue risk

A telecom team wants to know which customer groups show more cancellations and where retention outreach may be worth testing.

- How does churn vary across contract type and tenure?
- How much recurring monthly revenue is associated with customers who leave?
- Which active segments have higher observed churn?

The project dataset is **simulated**, not company evidence.

```{r}
#| label: setup-data
#| include: false
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

raw_customers <- read_csv("data/customer_churn_simulated.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
contract_medians <- raw_customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(contract_median = median(monthly_charge, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
customers <- raw_customers |>
  left_join(contract_medians, by = "contract") |>
  mutate(
    monthly_charge = if_else(is.na(monthly_charge), contract_median, monthly_charge),
    contract = factor(contract, levels = c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year")),
    churn_flag = as.integer(churn == "Yes"),
    monthly_revenue = monthly_charge
  )
by_contract <- customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(
    customers = n(),
    churned = sum(churn_flag),
    churn_rate = mean(churn_flag),
    churned_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 1]),
    active_mrr = sum(monthly_revenue[churn_flag == 0]),
    exposure = active_mrr * churn_rate,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

::: notes
[45 sec] This is descriptive analysis for prioritizing investigation—not proof of why people churn.
:::

## The data-to-decision workflow

1. Import the CSV and inspect rows, columns, types, and missingness.
2. Clean categories and fill missing monthly charges with the median within contract type; record the count.
3. Create tenure bands and a binary churn flag.
4. Summarize rates and revenue by contract and tenure.
5. Visualize segment rates and monthly revenue exposure.

Each step is executable and explained in `analysis/churn_analysis.qmd`.

::: notes
[45 sec] The imputation rule preserves within-plan price differences better than one overall median. Imputation remains an assumption to disclose.
:::

## A readable analysis chunk

```r
customers |>
  group_by(contract) |>
  summarise(
    customers = n(),
    churn_rate = mean(churn == "Yes"),
    churned_mrr = sum(monthly_charge[churn == "Yes"]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The rate is the share of rows in each contract group marked as churned. `churned_mrr` is their monthly charge total at cancellation, **not a forecast of annual loss**.

::: notes
[55 sec] Talk through `group_by`, `summarise`, and the denominator. Use rendered tables when presenting. This is not a causal or predictive model.
:::

## Visualize patterns, then interpret carefully

```{r}
#| label: churn-charts
#| echo: false
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(by_contract, aes(contract, churn_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2C6E8F", width = .65) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", customers)), vjust = -0.4, size = 4.6) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), limits = c(0, .27)) +
  labs(title = "Churn rate (share of customers)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)

ggplot(by_contract, aes(contract, exposure)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#B36B35", width = .65) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Illustrative exposure (USD per month)", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 16)
```

**Exposure** = active segment MRR × observed churn rate: a scenario for ranking priorities, not a calibrated forecast.

::: notes
[50 sec] Left: proportions, with the denominator n above each bar. Right: the same rates translated into money. Month-to-month leads on both here, but in real data the two rankings can differ, so name each measure and look at rate, segment size and money together.
:::

## Result snapshot from the simulated run {.smaller}

Calculated during rendering, after the contract-specific median imputation (fixed-seed synthetic sample).

```{r}
#| echo: false
by_contract |>
  transmute(
    contract, customers, churned,
    churn_rate = scales::percent(churn_rate, accuracy = 0.1),
    churned_mrr = scales::dollar(churned_mrr, prefix = "USD ", accuracy = 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Contract", "Customers", "Churned",
                             "Churn rate", "Observed churned MRR"))
```

Month-to-month leads on rate and churned MRR. Two-year above one-year? With only 97 two-year customers, that gap is sampling noise. Descriptive outputs, not evidence about a real operator.

::: notes
[40 sec] The fixed-seed synthetic file produces 72 churned out of 330 month-to-month customers (21.8%), compared with 6.9% and 10.3% in the other groups. The table is computed in the document after imputation. Simulation rules create these associations. Likely question: why is two-year (10.3 %) above one-year (6.9 %) although the generator lowers two-year churn? Answer: only 97 two-year customers; 10 vs. 12 churners. The 95 % intervals (about 5–19 % and 4–12 %) overlap widely, so this is sampling noise, not a finding. Small segments need intervals, not just point estimates.
:::

## What the results can and cannot say

**Can say:** in this generated sample, churn rates and revenue exposure differ across recorded groups.

**Cannot say:** contract type or support history caused cancellation, or that an offer will prevent it.

Selection, measurement, omitted variables, and simulation rules limit generalization. Validate on real data and test interventions [@hubercourse].

::: notes
[45 sec] Separate association from causation. Sensible next steps are validating definitions, investigating service issues, and testing a retention offer with a comparison group.
:::

## Takeaways and class exercise

- Literate programming joins explanation, code, and computed output.
- Quarto renders; R computes; RStudio supports the workflow.
- Reproducibility needs documented data, decisions, software, and inspection.
- In the exercise, compare churn by contract and explain one limitation.

[35 sec] Close with `exercise/Churn_Exercise.qmd`. Planned speaking time: about 11–13 minutes, excluding the exercise.
:::
